summary: Provides a collection of schema elements for LDAP drawn from the COSINE and Internet X.500 pilot projects. It replaces RFC 1274 and updates RFC 2247 and RFC 2798. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: An old set of entry types and fields from early directory experiments, updated so it can still be used.

what is the ldap mail attribute
subtitle: A cleaned-up set of directory attributes and object classes inherited from the COSINE and Internet X.500 pilots, rewritten for LDAP.

tldr.problem: Many schema elements from the early 1990s COSINE and X.500 pilots were in wide use, but the old descriptions in RFC 1274 could not be used without adaptation, which risked interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4524 gives modern LDAP schema descriptions for 25 widely used attribute types and nine object classes, and lists which old elements were left behind.
tldr.outcome: Together with RFC 4519 and RFC 4517 it obsoletes RFC 1274 in its entirety, and it updates RFC 2247 and RFC 2798.

today: RFC 4524 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2006. It obsoletes RFC 1274 and updates RFC 2247 and RFC 2798, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why the COSINE Schema Was Refreshed
sections.content:
In the late 1980s the CCITT standardized X.500 Directory Services. Directory piloting followed in the early 1990s, including the COSINE PARADISE project in Europe. To support large pilots, RFC 1274 standardized a directory schema and naming architecture.

Since then LDAP arrived and X.500 evolved. Much of RFC 1274 was superseded by ITU-T Recommendations and other RFCs, yet many of its schema elements are in wide use and lack standardized descriptions for modern X.500 and LDAP directories. Because the old descriptions cannot be used without adaptation, interoperability issues may arise. RFC 4524 supplies standardized descriptions where needed.

The document takes over from several others. Together with RFC 4519 and RFC 4517 it obsoletes RFC 1274 in its entirety. Its description of the domain object class replaces Section 5.2 of RFC 2247, and with RFC 4519 it replaces Section 9.1.3 of RFC 2798. Elements not brought forward are to be regarded as Historic.
sections.plainLanguage: Some old directory forms were still used everywhere, but their instructions were written for a very old system. This document rewrites the instructions so everyone fills the forms in the same way.

sections.title: The Attribute Types
sections.content:
An attribute type describes one kind of fact stored in a directory entry. Each one is written in the LDAP description format with an object identifier, a matching rule for equality and substring searches, and a syntax. The attributes fall into a few groups.

  • People and contact data: homePhone, homePostalAddress, mobile, pager, mail, personalTitle, drink, manager and secretary.
  • Documents: documentAuthor, documentIdentifier, documentLocation, documentPublisher, documentTitle and documentVersion.
  • Places and domains: associatedDomain, associatedName, buildingName, co (the friendly country name) and roomNumber.
  • Classification: host, info, organizationalStatus, uniqueIdentifier and userClass.

Several attributes carry caveats. The directory does not check that associatedDomain or mail values follow the domain or Mailbox grammar; that is the application's job, and applications supporting internationalized domain names SHALL use the ToASCII method. The mail attribute is compared with caseIgnoreIA5Match, so the assertion (mail=joe@example.com) matches JOE@example.com even though the local parts differ, and two mailboxes differing only by case of the local part cannot both be stored.

Other notes: values of homePostalAddress should be limited to up to 6 directory strings of 30 characters each, though the directory need not enforce it. Applications should not attach specific meaning to info; the description attribute exists for that. The uniqueIdentifier attribute defined here must not be confused with X.520's attribute, which LDAP calls x500UniqueIdentifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute is one labeled box on a form, like "home phone" or "room number". The document says what kind of thing goes in each box and how to compare two answers.

sections.title: The Object Classes
sections.content:
An object class says which attributes an entry must have (MUST) and which it may have (MAY). RFC 4524 defines nine of them.

  • account: a computer account. It requires uid, which SHOULD be used for naming.
  • document: a document. It requires documentIdentifier.
  • documentSeries: a series of documents such as the Request For Comments memos. It requires cn.
  • domain: a DNS domain for things that are not organizations or other more specific kinds of object. It requires dc, which should be used for naming.
  • domainRelatedObject: an auxiliary class for entries whose DNS domain is equivalent to an X.500 domain such as an organization. It requires associatedDomain.
  • friendlyCountry: a subclass of country that adds a friendlier name through the required co attribute.
  • rFC822LocalPart: the local part of an Internet mail address, treated as a domain object.
  • room: a room. It requires cn, which SHOULD be used for naming.
  • simpleSecurityObject: an auxiliary class that forces an entry to have a userPassword when its structural class does not require or allow one.

Most are structural classes that stand on their own. The two auxiliary classes, domainRelatedObject and simpleSecurityObject, are added to an entry alongside its main class.
sections.plainLanguage: An object class is a whole form made of boxes. A "room" form must have a name box filled in, and may also have a phone number or notes box.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The general LDAP security considerations of RFC 4510 apply to this schema, and extra notes appear where relevant above. Directory administrators should restrict access to sensitive information to authorized entities and use data integrity and confidentiality services to protect against eavesdropping.

Simple authentication such as plain text passwords should only be used when adequate data security services are in place. The RFC notes that LDAP offers reasonably strong authentication and data security services.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone book can hold private details. Keep the private pages locked up, and do not shout your password across a crowded room.

sections.title: IANA Registry Updates
sections.content:
IANA has updated the LDAP descriptors registry so that the descriptors defined here point to RFC 4524. The list covers both the primary names, such as account and associatedDomain, and alternative names such as favouriteDrink and rfc822Mailbox.

The alternative names are marked with an asterisk in the template, which means the registration is historic in nature. The registry template names the IESG as the change controller.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of names that everyone shares. The list was updated so each name points to this new document.

sections.title: What Changed Since RFC 1274
sections.content:
The document calls itself a substantial rewrite of RFC 1274. Some X.500 names have shorter LDAP names, for example favoriteDrink is drink and rfc822Mailbox is mail. Some implementations may still recognize the X.500 name for legacy reasons, so those names are reserved for that purpose only.

Several things were not brought forward. pilotObject was largely replaced by operational attributes from X.500(93) and LDAPv3. pilotPerson was largely replaced by organizationalPerson and subclasses such as inetOrgPerson. The dNSDomain class, and pilotDSA and qualityLabelledData, were left out because their use is primarily experimental.

The old caseIgnoreIA5StringSyntax was replaced by the IA5String syntax with suitable matching rules. The old restriction that mail values have non-zero length is no longer reflected in the syntax, although values should still be proper mailboxes. From RFC 2247, the domainNameForm name form was not brought forward because name forms are left to a future specification.
sections.plainLanguage: When you rewrite a book you keep the useful chapters and drop the ones nobody reads. Some old forms were kept with shorter names, and a few were thrown away.
